Asia
ā'zhä
n. (in the New Testament, the Roman province of proconsular Asia in western Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city and the seven churches within it)
From Greek Asia, the Roman provincial name for the western third of Asia Minor. In Scripture it never means the continent; the boundaries are Roman and administrative, and the KJV keeps the ancient sense.

Biblical Definition

Asia in the New Testament is a province, not a continent — the western coastland of Asia Minor with Ephesus at its head. It is the field of the most fruitful stretch of Paul's labour. Barred by the Spirit from preaching there on the second journey (Act 16:6), he was later given the whole province at once: teaching daily in the school of Tyrannus, “this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks” (Act 19:10). Even the silversmiths admitted the scale of it — “almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people” (Act 19:26). Out of that harvest came the seven churches to whom the risen Christ dictates letters: “John to the seven churches which are in Asia” (Rev 1:4). But Asia is also the province of the sharpest sorrow in the epistles. Writing near the end, Paul records a mass defection: “all they which are in Asia be turned away from me” (2Ti 1:15). The same ground gives the dictionary both pictures at once — a whole province hearing the word in two years, and the same province cooling within a generation, with Ephesus itself charged by the Lord to remember whence it had fallen.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Asia as one of the great divisions of the earth; in the New Testament the name denotes the Roman province of that name in Asia Minor.

expand to see more

ASIA, n. One of the great continents or quarters of the globe, lying east of Europe and north of the Indian ocean.

In the New Testament the word is used in a narrower sense, for the Roman province of proconsular Asia.

That province comprehended Mysia, Lydia, Caria and part of Phrygia, and its capital was Ephesus.

The seven churches to which the Revelation was addressed were all within this province.

Paul laboured there three years, and all that dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord.

Key Scripture

Act 19:10 — "And this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks."

Act 19:26 — "Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:"

Rev 1:4 — "John to the seven churches which are in Asia: Grace be unto you, and peace, from him which is, and which was, and which is to come; and from the seven Spirits which are before his throne;"

2Ti 1:15 — "This thou knowest, that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me; of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes."

Modern Corruption

The rapid evangelization of Asia is copied as a technique, and the equally rapid cooling of Asia is left out of the copy — producing a method for gathering crowds with no doctrine of perseverance attached.

expand to see more

Acts 19 is a favourite text for church-growth strategy: two years, one hall, a whole province reached. What the strategy literature seldom carries over is 2 Timothy 1:15 and Revelation 2:4, where the same province turns away from the apostle and the same flagship church is charged with leaving its first love. The dictionary insists on holding the two together. Paul's own account of his method in Asia was not a technique but a labour: three years of warning “every one night and day with tears” (Act 20:31), and a farewell that predicted grievous wolves entering in among them. A ministry model drawn from the crowds and not from the tears has taken the wrong half.

There is a second and older confusion, harmless in itself but worth naming: reading “Asia” here as the continent. It makes the sentence in Acts 19:10 into something the text does not claim and hands the sceptic an easy charge of exaggeration. Luke is a precise writer using Roman administrative terms exactly as a first-century reader would — Asia beside Mysia, Bithynia, Galatia and Cilicia, each a real jurisdiction with a real boundary. That precision is itself evidence. A later legend-maker would not have known the provincial map well enough to use it so casually and so correctly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Asia (G773), Asia; Ephesos (G2181), Ephesus; logos (G3056), word; ekklesia (G1577), church, assembly; apostrepho (G654), to turn away.

expand to see more

Greek Asia (G773) — Asia; the Roman province of western Asia Minor, not the continent.

Greek Ephesos (G2181) — Ephesus; its chief city and the base of Paul's three-year labour.

Greek ekklesia (G1577) — assembly, church; the seven of Revelation all stood in this province.

Greek apostrepho (G654) — to turn away, desert; the verb of the defection in 2Ti 1:15.

Greek anthupatos (G446) — proconsul, deputy; the officer of a senatorial province such as Asia.

Usage

"“All they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus” — two years, one province."

"“All they which are in Asia be turned away from me” — the same province, one generation."

"“The seven churches which are in Asia” — the harvest, addressed by the risen Christ Himself."
